# Final Touches — Murim Login

## Goal

Prepare one mastered chapter for readers. This pass adds footnotes, repairs formatting, and fixes duplicate or missing sentences. It is not a fluency rewrite.

Keep the mastered prose. Change a sentence only to attach a footnote, repair System / thought / speech / chat formatting, restore a source sentence the English dropped, remove an English sentence the Korean does not support, or fix a character's name or pronoun as described below.

## Names and pronouns

The packet lists the profiled characters named in this chapter with their gender, and any required name corrections.

- Use the glossary or character-card English for every name. Apply each required name correction everywhere it occurs.
- Korean usually omits pronouns. When a card gives `female` or `male` and the English uses the other pronoun for that character, fix the pronoun. Leave pronouns alone for a character whose gender is `unknown`.

## Duplicates and omissions

Compare the English with the Korean source.

- Restore source facts, events, dialogue, and sentences the English dropped, in the same place in the scene.
- Remove English sentences that have no support in the Korean.
- Keep a bold label that names a quoted document, manual, warning, or sign, such as `> **Warning**`. Keep it when this chapter recalls or reprints a notice that was labeled earlier, even if the Korean reprint shows only the body.
- Keep repetition the Korean itself repeats: comedy, panic, emphasis, echoed dialogue, and short beats such as `……`.
- Do not treat a short refrain or a deliberate echo as a duplicate.

## Footnotes

Use Markdown footnotes (`[^1]`, `[^2]`, …). Number them in order of first appearance, starting at 1 for this chapter. Put every definition in one block at the end of the file.

Within this chapter, write one definition for a term, unit, amount, or reference. Every later occurrence of that same thing reuses the same marker. `goshiwon` five times is one note, and so is `hyung`. A different amount or a different term gets its own note. Another chapter may carry its own note for the same term.

Write notes in factual English. No spoilers and no jokes added by the note. Romanize words. A note may include the original character when it is explaining that character. Keep Hangul jamo already used as chat reactions, such as ㅋㅋ and ㄷㄷ.

Never write a footnote whose job is to identify or describe a story character, creature, pet, group, place, item, or plot event. The story introduces its own cast; a note must not say who someone is, what they did, or what a name refers to inside the story. This holds even when the glossary or a character card explains the name: those are reference for you, not footnote material.

When a story name coincides with a real person, brand, or work (Magic Johnson, Mimi), the name is the story's. Do not footnote the real one unless the Korean source itself makes that reference.

Add a note only when an English reader would otherwise miss the meaning or the conversion. Skip it when the sentence already says what the reference means. A translated proverb whose warning is plain, a joke the next line completes, a place name used as a place, and a fictional law the dialogue already describes do not get notes.

Skip a conversion footnote when the prose already states both metric and imperial for that quantity.

### Won

Footnote Korean won, including round figures and vague amounts (“hundreds of millions of won”), when the prose does not already give the conversion. Use only the project rates in the packet. Show dollars, then euros, as approximate figures. Round large amounts to about two significant figures and say “about.” For a vague amount, give the approximate range those words cover. One note per distinct amount; reuse it for every later mention of that same amount.

Do not convert traditional money (nyang, taels, cash) or Chinese yuan with the won rate. Explain those with a cultural or historical note only when the English does not already carry the meaning.

### Units

Footnote a Korean or Chinese traditional unit, or a metric quantity, once in the chapter, with both metric and imperial, using this table:

| Unit | Use | Metric | Imperial |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| pyeong (평) | area | 3.31 m² | 35.6 ft² |
| geun (근) | Korean weight | 600 g | 1.32 lb |
| ja / cheok (자) | length | 30.3 cm | 11.9 in |
| chi (치) | length | 3.03 cm | 1.19 in |
| don (돈) | weight | 3.75 g | 0.132 oz |
| gwan (관) | weight | 3.75 kg | 8.27 lb |
| ri (리), Korea | distance | 393 m | 0.244 mi |
| li (里), China | distance | 500 m | 0.311 mi |
| jin (斤), modern Chinese | weight | 500 g | 1.10 lb |
| liang (两), modern Chinese | weight | 50 g | 1.76 oz |

Choose Korean ri or Chinese li from the setting. Say which one the note uses.

Also footnote metric quantities already in the English (kilometers, meters, centimeters, kilograms, grams, liters, square meters, degrees Celsius) with the imperial equivalent. Use unit words or abbreviations (`ft`, `in`, `mi`, `lb`, `oz`, `gal`). Do not use `"` or `'` as unit marks.

### Cultural references

Footnote a Korean, Chinese, or other Asian word, custom, institution, food, joke, or allusion when the English does not already carry it: `goshiwon`, `hyung`, `doenjang`, `jeonse`. Explain it in one or two sentences. One note per term in the chapter, reused by every later occurrence.

Leave it unnoted when the English is already clear. Do not explain a proverb the translation has already stated, a pun the scene completes, or ordinary vocabulary.

Do not footnote standing series vocabulary. Never add a note whose job is to define any of these, including ordinary variants and compounds:

- Murim
- qi, including demonic qi, innate qi, and qi deviation
- dantian, including the Upper, Middle, and Lower Dantian
- internal energy
- mana

A note about something else may mention these words. Do not attach a marker to them.

## Formatting

Enforce these four patterns. Repair System, speech, thought, and chat formatting when it drifts. Leave every other blockquote heading as it stands.

- **System.** Each real game System panel is one Markdown blockquote headed exactly `> **System**`. Keep the panel’s lines inside that blockquote. Start a new panel only when prose intervenes. Keep every `> **System**` panel from the mastered chapter, including a notice the narrator only hears. Do not turn a panel into italics, a sound effect, or narration. Do not repeat a panel. A notice the mastered chapter already shows more than once stays repeated that many times, and no more. Do not wrap System text in square brackets or label a manual, sign, or ordinary quotation as System. A manual or remembered notice keeps its own label, such as `> **Warning**` or `> **Product User Manual**`. That label is not a System panel, and it is not drift.
- **Speech.** Spoken dialogue uses curly double quotes (`“` `”`). Not straight quotes, not italics.
- **Thoughts.** Direct thoughts are italics with no quotation marks. Keep a mastered thought in italics. Do not turn it into spoken dialogue.
- **Chat and comments.** Public comment threads and private chat logs shown as threads are one blockquote. Each message line begins with `└`, as in `> └ **Name:** message`. Keep a thread title that is not itself a message, such as `> **Peace Guild**`, on its own line above the messages. Do not add a `**Chat**` heading. A status line that is only a name or level, such as `> **Lv. 22 Hyuk Mujin**`, is not a chat message. Leave that line unchanged, including the bold. Ordinary spoken dialogue stays in curly quotes.
- **Headings.** The only Markdown heading is `# Chapter N`. Do not add `##` or `###`. A diary title or similar label stays a bold line, `**Training Day 1**`, even when the mastered copy used a smaller heading.

Leave narration as narration. Scene breaks stay `* * *`, with the same count as the source.

## Output contract

Return only the complete English Markdown chapter. The first nonblank line must be `# Chapter N`. No status line and no model preamble. Do not add Hangul syllables. Chat jamo and a character cited in a note may stay.

## Project conversion rates

These rates are binding. Do not look up or substitute a market rate.

- 1 US dollar = 1400 Korean won
- 1 euro = 1550 Korean won

Convert every won amount with these rates. In each footnote, give dollars first and euros second.

For ages, people had called the lands north and south of the Yellow River the Central Plains and considered them the heart of the world.

The birthplace of the earliest civilization. Fertile land, abundant resources, and the staggering productivity they made possible.

With advantages like those, people were bound to flock there from every direction.

The problem was that among them were foreign peoples from distant borderlands, who often wanted to “borrow” the Central Plains’ gold and silver treasures.

By their own methods: plunder or occupation.

Naturally, the people of the Central Plains weren’t too fond of that.

So they built the Great Wall, stretching a full ten thousand li.[^1] They strengthened the armies stationed along the borders, raised impregnable fortresses and walled cities throughout the land, and kept reinforcing them generation after generation.

All the more so in Xining, the capital of Qinghai—the farthest of the borderlands, practically the continent’s GOP.[^2]

But the rulers who gave those orders, and the craftsmen and laborers who sweated to carry them out, could never have dreamed there were madmen who would hurl themselves bodily against walls built of solid stone, stacked layer upon layer and sealed tight with lime.

Or that those madmen would be enormous monsters, hideous and monstrously strong.

*Rumble, rumble!*

The ground—or rather, the city—shook.

Several thousand monsters battered the wall with their bare bodies or with huge logs and clubs they’d gotten from who knew where. The sight alone was enough to freeze the blood.

It doused the defenders’ fighting spirit just as it had begun to blaze.

“Hah…!”

“Don’t break formation! Hold your positions!”

Choked breaths escaped here and there amid a storm of shouted commands.

And this wasn’t happening only at the West Gate, where I was stationed.

The North Gate and South Gate were the same. So was the East Gate, though the assault there was comparatively light.

Countless enemies had encircled Xining for dozens of li.[^1] Now, with those stubbornly resilient monsters in front, they were beginning their siege in earnest.

“Archers, ready!”

“Loose! Loose!”

*Shhk, thud-thud!*

Our response was swift, too.

A dense rain of arrows fell at nearly direct-fire angles, holding back the Dark Heaven followers, while we brought out the countermeasure we’d prepared for the monsters.

“Is it ready?”

One of the commanders answered my quiet question. Sweat had already soaked the inside of his helmet.

“Everything’s prepared, just as the Marquis of Shangshan ordered.”

Then there was no need to hesitate any longer.

I turned to the tense commander and the imperial troops standing by.

“Pour it all out. Give them the works.”

The moment I gave the order—

*Groan.*

Signal flags swung vigorously. With a heavy metallic groan, the great iron cauldrons set along the wall tipped and disgorged their contents.

Thick, black, boiling oil.

*Splash! Ssssss!*

—*GRAAAAH!*

Acrid smoke mingled with the smell of burning, and the monsters’ screams rose over it all.

But I knew better than anyone that oil alone wouldn’t be enough to destroy creatures that were practically undead monsters already.

And with the sorcerers controlling them still nowhere to be seen, this was the right moment for me to act.

*Fwoosh.*

I drew a deep breath, and the fire dragon coiled deep inside me awoke.

It had left its longtime home in my Lower Dantian. Now the enormous flame had made a nest atop the peak of my Middle Dantian, a peak that touched the heavens. It stirred and flowed into every part of my body.

Endlessly. Fiercely.

And at the same time, as swiftly as a ray of light.

*Whoosh.*

The moment I stepped forward, a spine-chilling sensation of weightlessness swept through me.

Before I knew it, everything lay beneath my feet.

The city wall, rising a dozen or so jang[^3] like a barrier at the edge of the world. The monsters and fanatics blackening the ground below.

Only one thing was level with my eyes.

A spear, wreathed in the flames of dark blue Force.

*Grind.*

Every muscle in my body drew taut as a bowstring. My senses, sharper than ever, focused at my fingertips.

I sought the most destructive, most perfect path for the spear to take as it cut slowly through the air and plunged down.

*Now.*

With that thought, I sent White Flame hurtling toward the distant ground.

*Whoosh!*

A flash of light. Through the air warped by searing heat, a streak of dark blue flame slipped among the enemies near the wall.

Then came a roar like the sky splitting open.

*BOOM!*

A vast pillar of fire surged up along the wall, defying the heavy rain pouring down without end.

Beneath it lay ground soaked with the oil we’d poured out so freely—and the enemies’ flesh and bones.

“Ghk, aaagh!”

“Keugh…!”

For better or worse, enemies who had barely escaped death were engulfed in flames and let out terrible screams.

Hundreds of them, at a rough count.

Maybe more.

But before the enormous roar that had shaken heaven and earth could even fade, my body was already dropping over their heads.

*Bang! Bang! Ba-bang!*

The air burst beneath my feet with each successive step.

The ground that had seemed impossibly far away rushed toward me. I reached into the empty air, where only wind and rain whipped past.

*Inventory open. Summon.*

*Ding.*

A System notification sounded, and something solid filled my empty hand. The enemies who had rushed toward the spot where I was descending from the sky stared wide-eyed.

“What the—”

*Shhk!*

One stroke, two halves.

The enemies proved those four words with their lives as their bodies split left and right.

A fountain of blood, vivid red even beneath the dark sky, spurted up. Madness glinted in the eyes of the enemies, already losing their focus.

“Heaven above and earth below, all demons bow!”

“Attack!”

*Shh-shh-shhk!*

A wind of blades swept in, colder than the rain.

The enemies had me surrounded on all sides, from every direction, and rushed in without regard for their lives.

Like moths drawn helplessly toward a flame.

*Shhk!*

Sharp Sword Energy slashed in from all sides.

Every streak was blood-red and looked dangerously unstable, as though its wielder had reached into a realm he had no business touching. Yet their power and speed rivaled a Peak master’s.

I still remembered seeing the same thing before.

*Temporary Strength Pills.*

A person’s final flame, fed with their own life.

I knew how tremendous the pills’ effects were, even if they lasted only a short time. Their danger matched their power.

I also knew that their hastily stacked kindling couldn’t match the heat of the furnace I’d built by surviving countless brushes with death.

*Thump!*

To conserve my strength, I hadn’t put so much as a trace of internal energy into the blow.

It was enough.

My body had already surpassed human limits by several steps. My senses, honed in the face of death, made it possible.

*Grrk.*

The Dark Heaven follower clutched at his throat, split open in an instant. By then, I’d already passed him and leaped toward the others.

*Whoosh!*

Half a step left.

Three streaks of Sword Energy missed me by a hair and tangled in midair. The rough broad-bladed saber that had been rusting in Xining’s armory left my hand.

*Wham!*

Without an ounce of internal energy behind it, the blade spun with sheer, terrifying force and cut through three necks.

No—it smashed through them.

At the same time, a command rang out in my mind, and new blades appeared in both hands.

A straight sword in my left. A narrow-bladed sword in my right.

They were unfamiliar. Yet somehow, impossibly familiar.

*Shreeeek! Thud-thud!*

Just the right amount of strength and speed, guided by movements that followed the flow of battle.

I fell into a Trance and swept through the enemies beneath the wall. Each swing of my sword and saber brought blood and screams. With every step, corpses spread beneath my feet like a carpet.

*Come.*

I spared even the single breath I might have let out without thinking.

With that single thought, I cut down the enemies surging at me from every direction. I cut and kept cutting.

I dodged a thrusting sword and pierced its wielder’s heart with the narrow-bladed sword. With nothing but a straight sword gone red with rust, I controlled the blades of five swords imbued with Sword Energy.

*Clang-clang-clang!*

I pressed against the flats of their blades and twisted. That was enough to knock the swords into one another in a tangle and cut off their wielders’ breath.

Strength when strength was needed. Softness when softness was needed.

When the narrow-bladed sword broke, I summoned an axe from the nearly infinite storeroom of my Inventory. With the broken straight sword, I wielded a blade technique infused with the principles of the Flame Divine Palm.

Even I couldn’t understand it. In that moment, I was free of every restriction and limit.

And suddenly, I understood.

*So that’s what he meant.*

Jeok Cheongang had once told me that when one’s understanding of martial arts reached a certain realm, every living, moving thing became a martial art.

Even a weak, bending reed would be no different from a Divine Sword.

Of course, I hadn’t reached that realm. But at last, I felt I could faintly grasp what he’d meant.

*Shhk!*

With the sensation of death running through my fingertips, I started to turn toward another enemy—then blinked.

There was no one. Everything was quiet.

The Dark Heaven followers who had taken Temporary Strength Pills. The enormous monsters that could no longer be called human.

Beneath the western wall, I was the only one left standing on two feet.

The blood-soaked scene before me meant one thing.

I had wiped out the enemy vanguard, at least a thousand strong.

All by myself.

*Ding. Ding. Ding.*

>
> **Intimidation** rises significantly!
>

System notifications poured into my ears like a dam breaking. A tremendous cheer erupted from atop the wall.

Then—

*BWOOOOO!*

A horn sounded with a deep note that made me shudder. At its call, Dark Heaven’s main force—some hundred thousand strong—began advancing toward the city walls.

And I realized what their movement meant.

“……!”

The monsters.

No—the giants.

Each stood well over a jang[^3] tall. Their corpses had already piled halfway up the wall.

# Final Touches — Murim Login

## Goal

Prepare one mastered chapter for readers. This pass adds footnotes, repairs formatting, and fixes duplicate or missing sentences. It is not a fluency rewrite.

Keep the mastered prose. Change a sentence only to attach a footnote, repair System / thought / speech / chat formatting, restore a source sentence the English dropped, remove an English sentence the Korean does not support, or fix a character's name or pronoun as described below.

## Names and pronouns

The packet lists the profiled characters named in this chapter with their gender, and any required name corrections.

- Use the glossary or character-card English for every name. Apply each required name correction everywhere it occurs.
- Korean usually omits pronouns. When a card gives `female` or `male` and the English uses the other pronoun for that character, fix the pronoun. Leave pronouns alone for a character whose gender is `unknown`.

## Duplicates and omissions

Compare the English with the Korean source.

- Restore source facts, events, dialogue, and sentences the English dropped, in the same place in the scene.
- Remove English sentences that have no support in the Korean.
- Keep a bold label that names a quoted document, manual, warning, or sign, such as `> **Warning**`. Keep it when this chapter recalls or reprints a notice that was labeled earlier, even if the Korean reprint shows only the body.
- Keep repetition the Korean itself repeats: comedy, panic, emphasis, echoed dialogue, and short beats such as `……`.
- Do not treat a short refrain or a deliberate echo as a duplicate.

## Footnotes

Use Markdown footnotes (`[^1]`, `[^2]`, …). Number them in order of first appearance, starting at 1 for this chapter. Put every definition in one block at the end of the file.

Within this chapter, write one definition for a term, unit, amount, or reference. Every later occurrence of that same thing reuses the same marker. `goshiwon` five times is one note, and so is `hyung`. A different amount or a different term gets its own note. Another chapter may carry its own note for the same term.

Write notes in factual English. No spoilers and no jokes added by the note. Romanize words. A note may include the original character when it is explaining that character. Keep Hangul jamo already used as chat reactions, such as ㅋㅋ and ㄷㄷ.

Never write a footnote whose job is to identify or describe a story character, creature, pet, group, place, item, or plot event. The story introduces its own cast; a note must not say who someone is, what they did, or what a name refers to inside the story. This holds even when the glossary or a character card explains the name: those are reference for you, not footnote material.

When a story name coincides with a real person, brand, or work (Magic Johnson, Mimi), the name is the story's. Do not footnote the real one unless the Korean source itself makes that reference.

Add a note only when an English reader would otherwise miss the meaning or the conversion. Skip it when the sentence already says what the reference means. A translated proverb whose warning is plain, a joke the next line completes, a place name used as a place, and a fictional law the dialogue already describes do not get notes.

Skip a conversion footnote when the prose already states both metric and imperial for that quantity.

Footnote Korean won, including round figures and vague amounts (“hundreds of millions of won”), when the prose does not already give the conversion. Use only the project rates in the packet. Keep every `> **System**` panel from the mastered chapter, including a notice the narrator only hears. Do not turn a panel into italics, a sound effect, or narration. Do not repeat a panel. A notice the mastered chapter already shows more than once stays repeated that many times, and no more. Do not wrap System text in square brackets or label a manual, sign, or ordinary quotation as System. A manual or remembered notice keeps its own label, such as `> **Warning**` or `> **Product User Manual**`. That label is not a System panel, and it is not drift.
- **Speech.** Spoken dialogue uses curly double quotes (`“` `”`). Not straight quotes, not italics.
- **Thoughts.** Direct thoughts are italics with no quotation marks. Keep a mastered thought in italics. Do not turn it into spoken dialogue.

Keep a thread title that is not itself a message, such as `> **Peace Guild**`, on its own line above the messages. Do not add a `**Chat**` heading. A status line that is only a name or level, such as `> **Lv. 22 Hyuk Mujin**`, is not a chat message. Leave that line unchanged, including the bold. Ordinary spoken dialogue stays in curly quotes.
- **Headings.** The only Markdown heading is `# Chapter N`. Do not add `##` or `###`. A diary title or similar label stays a bold line, `**Training Day 1**`, even when the mastered copy used a smaller heading.

Leave narration as narration. Scene breaks stay `* * *`, with the same count as the source.

Return only the complete English Markdown chapter. The first nonblank line must be `# Chapter N`. No status line and no model preamble. Do not add Hangul syllables. Chat jamo and a character cited in a note may stay.

- 1 euro = 1550 Korean won

For ages, people had called the lands north and south of the Yellow River the Central Plains and considered them the heart of the world.

The birthplace of the earliest civilization. Fertile land, abundant resources, and the staggering productivity they made possible.

With advantages like those, people were bound to flock there from every direction.

By their own methods: plunder or occupation.

All the more so in Xining, the capital of Qinghai—the farthest of the borderlands, practically the continent’s GOP.

But the rulers who gave those orders, and the craftsmen and laborers who sweated to carry them out, could never have dreamed there were madmen who would hurl themselves bodily against walls built of solid stone, stacked layer upon layer and sealed tight with lime.

Or that those madmen would be enormous monsters, hideous and monstrously strong.

*Rumble, rumble!*

The ground—or rather, the city—shook.

Several thousand monsters battered the wall with their bare bodies or with huge logs and clubs they’d gotten from who knew where. The sight alone was enough to freeze the blood.

It doused the defenders’ fighting spirit just as it had begun to blaze.

“Hah…!”

“Don’t break formation! Hold your positions!”

Choked breaths escaped here and there amid a storm of shouted commands.

And this wasn’t happening only at the West Gate, where I was stationed.

The North Gate and South Gate were the same. So was the East Gate, though the assault there was comparatively light.

Countless enemies had encircled Xining for dozens of li. Now, with those stubbornly resilient monsters in front, they were beginning their siege in earnest.

“Archers, ready!”

“Loose! Loose!”

*Shhk, thud-thud!*

Our response was swift, too.

A dense rain of arrows fell at nearly direct-fire angles, holding back the Dark Heaven followers, while we brought out the countermeasure we’d prepared for the monsters.

“Is it ready?”

One of the commanders answered my quiet question. Sweat had already soaked the inside of his helmet.

“Everything’s prepared, just as the Marquis of Shangshan ordered.”

Then there was no need to hesitate any longer.

I turned to the tense commander and the imperial troops standing by.

“Pour it all out. Give them the works.”

The moment I gave the order—

*Groan.*

Signal flags swung vigorously. With a heavy metallic groan, the great iron cauldrons set along the wall tipped and disgorged their contents.

Thick, black, boiling oil.

*Splash! Ssssss!*

—*GRAAAAH!*

Acrid smoke mingled with the smell of burning, and the monsters’ screams rose over it all.

But I knew better than anyone that oil alone wouldn’t be enough to destroy creatures that were practically undead monsters already.

And with the sorcerers controlling them still nowhere to be seen, this was the right moment for me to act.

*Fwoosh.*

I drew a deep breath, and the fire dragon coiled deep inside me awoke.

It had left its longtime home in my Lower Dantian. Now the enormous flame had made a nest atop the peak of my Middle Dantian, a peak that touched the heavens. It stirred and flowed into every part of my body.

Endlessly. Fiercely.

And at the same time, as swiftly as a ray of light.

*Whoosh.*

The moment I stepped forward, a spine-chilling sensation of weightlessness swept through me.

Before I knew it, everything lay beneath my feet.

The city wall, rising a dozen or so jang like a barrier at the edge of the world. The monsters and fanatics blackening the ground below.

Only one thing was level with my eyes.

A spear, wreathed in the flames of dark blue Force.

*Grind.*

Every muscle in my body drew taut as a bowstring. My senses, sharper than ever, focused at my fingertips.

I sought the most destructive, most perfect path for the spear to take as it cut slowly through the air and plunged down.

*Now.*

With that thought, I sent White Flame hurtling toward the distant ground.

*Whoosh!*

A flash of light. Through the air warped by searing heat, a streak of dark blue flame slipped among the enemies near the wall.

Then came a roar like the sky splitting open.

*BOOM!*

A vast pillar of fire surged up along the wall, defying the heavy rain pouring down without end.

Beneath it lay ground soaked with the oil we’d poured out so freely—and the enemies’ flesh and bones.

“Ghk, aaagh!”

“Keugh…!”

For better or worse, enemies who had barely escaped death were engulfed in flames and let out terrible screams.

Hundreds of them, at a rough count.

Maybe more.

But before the enormous roar that had shaken heaven and earth could even fade, my body was already dropping over their heads.

*Bang! Bang! Ba-bang!*

The air burst beneath my feet with each successive step.

The ground that had seemed impossibly far away rushed toward me. I reached into the empty air, where only wind and rain whipped past.

*Inventory open. Summon.*

*Ding.*

“What the—”

*Shhk!*

One stroke, two halves.

The enemies proved those four words with their lives as their bodies split left and right.

A fountain of blood, vivid red even beneath the dark sky, spurted up. Madness glinted in the eyes of the enemies, already losing their focus.

“Heaven above and earth below, all demons bow!”

“Attack!”

*Shh-shh-shhk!*

A wind of blades swept in, colder than the rain.

The enemies had me surrounded on all sides, from every direction, and rushed in without regard for their lives.

Like moths drawn helplessly toward a flame.

*Shhk!*

Sharp Sword Energy slashed in from all sides.

Every streak was blood-red and looked dangerously unstable, as though its wielder had reached into a realm he had no business touching. Yet their power and speed rivaled a Peak master’s.

I still remembered seeing the same thing before.

*Temporary Strength Pills.*

A person’s final flame, fed with their own life.

I knew how tremendous the pills’ effects were, even if they lasted only a short time. Their danger matched their power.

I also knew that their hastily stacked kindling couldn’t match the heat of the furnace I’d built by surviving countless brushes with death.

*Thump!*

To conserve my strength, I hadn’t put so much as a trace of internal energy into the blow.

My body had already surpassed human limits by several steps. My senses, honed in the face of death, made it possible.

*Grrk.*

The Dark Heaven follower clutched at his throat, split open in an instant. By then, I’d already passed him and leaped toward the others.

*Whoosh!*

Half a step left.

Three streaks of Sword Energy missed me by a hair and tangled in midair. The rough broad-bladed saber that had been rusting in Xining’s armory left my hand.

*Wham!*

Without an ounce of internal energy behind it, the blade spun with sheer, terrifying force and cut through three necks.

No—it smashed through them.

At the same time, a command rang out in my mind, and new blades appeared in both hands.

A straight sword in my left. A narrow-bladed sword in my right.

They were unfamiliar. Yet somehow, impossibly familiar.

*Shreeeek! Thud-thud!*

Just the right amount of strength and speed, guided by movements that followed the flow of battle.

*Come.*

I spared even the single breath I might have let out without thinking.

With that single thought, I cut down the enemies surging at me from every direction. I cut and kept cutting.

I dodged a thrusting sword and pierced its wielder’s heart with the narrow-bladed sword. With nothing but a straight sword gone red with rust, I controlled the blades of five swords imbued with Sword Energy.

*Clang-clang-clang!*

I pressed against the flats of their blades and twisted. That was enough to knock the swords into one another in a tangle and cut off their wielders’ breath.

Strength when strength was needed. Softness when softness was needed.

When the narrow-bladed sword broke, I summoned an axe from the nearly infinite storeroom of my Inventory. With the broken straight sword, I wielded a blade technique infused with the principles of the Flame Divine Palm.

Even I couldn’t understand it. In that moment, I was free of every restriction and limit.

And suddenly, I understood.

*So that’s what he meant.*

Jeok Cheongang had once told me that when one’s understanding of martial arts reached a certain realm, every living, moving thing became a martial art.

Even a weak, bending reed would be no different from a Divine Sword.

Of course, I hadn’t reached that realm. But at last, I felt I could faintly grasp what he’d meant.

*Shhk!*

With the sensation of death running through my fingertips, I started to turn toward another enemy—then blinked.

There was no one. Everything was quiet.

The Dark Heaven followers who had taken Temporary Strength Pills. The enormous monsters that could no longer be called human.

Beneath the western wall, I was the only one left standing on two feet.

The blood-soaked scene before me meant one thing.

I had wiped out the enemy vanguard, at least a thousand strong.

All by myself.
